newsitem.title: JAPAN: JAPAN'S BIG INSURERS CUT COSTS, BOOST DIVIDENDS.
newsitem.headline: JAPAN'S BIG INSURERS CUT COSTS, BOOST DIVIDENDS.

text.p: Japan's eight big life insurers said on Monday they were able to boost dividends to policy holders in the last fiscal year due to successful cost-cutting efforts, despite continued low yields on their investments.

The insurers were also aided by the disposal of bad loans and the cancellation of contracts with guaranteed payouts exceeding the meagre returns possible in last year's climate of low interest rates and falling stock prices.
The eight firms on Tuesday reported their earnings for the 1996/97 fiscal year ended March 31.
"After disposing of bad loans to (failed) housing loan companies, our non-performing loans fell sharply (in 1996/97)," said Minoru Mochida, senior managing director at Meiji Life Insurance Co.
He said that about 40 percent of Meiji's policy holders would get higher dividends in fiscal 1996/97 as a result of cost-cutting efforts and the bad loan disposals.
The results were less encouraging at Chiyoda Mutual Life Insurance Co, which said it would increase dividends for about 20 percent of its policy holders.
Unlike other big insurers who said they cut problem loans to manageable levels in 1996/97, Chiyoda said it would need another year to do so.
In 1996/97, the eight firms' premium income, equivalent to total revenues, fell by 5.4 percent to a combined 21.4 trillion yen ($191 billion) due to widespread cancellations of insurance contracts.

The insurers said that they cut the guaranteed rate of return in April 1996 on investments they managed for pension funds, which resulted in a withdrawal of pension fund contracts and boosted combined insurance payments by a total of 40.7 percent to 21.70 trillion yen ($193 billion) in 1996/97.

But the cancellations of high-yielding payout contracts had a positive impact on the insurers' balance sheets, narrowing the negative spread between low yields earned on their investments and the more generous returns promised to policy holders.
Average guaranteed rates of return fell to about four percent in 1996/97 from some five percent a year earlier.
Investment yields ranged from a low of 2.38 percent at Chiyoda to a high of 3.63 percent at Sumitomo Life Insurance Co, according to company executives.
The negative spread has weighed heavily on the insurers, which during the bubble of inflated asset prices in the late 1980s sold policies with high guaranteed rates of return.
But since the early 1990s, when the asset bubble burst, the economy slowed and interest rates fell, insurers have had trouble generating revenue to meet the guaranteed returns.
But a Sumitomo Life executive said yields were boosted at his company in 1996/97 by profitable securities sales.
The insurer also disposed of some 560 billion yen ($5.00 billion) in problem loans in 1996/97 and covered the disposals with profits from sales of property and securities, he said.

At the same time, however, the sharp decline in Japanese share prices in 1996/97 cut unrealised profits on shareholdings held by all eight of the firms, with the combined total falling by nearly half to 5.98 trillion yen ($53.3 billion) from 11.47 trillion yen ($102 billion) in 1995/96.
Medium-sized life insurers, including Toho Mutual Life Insurance Co, are to announce their annual results on Tuesday.
Financial markets are focusing on those firms' earnings after the failure earlier this year of another medium-sized insurer, Nissan Mutual Life Insurance Co, sent shockwaves through the markets.
Rating agency Standard & Poor's Corp last month assigned a Bpi rating to Toho and two other medium-sized insurers, indicating that their financial security is vulnerable.

The eight big life insurers which reported results on Monday are Meiji Life Insurance Co, Nippon Life Insurance Co, Dai-Ichi Mutual Life Insurance Co, Sumitomo Life Insurance Co, Asahi Mutual Life Insurance Co, Mitsui Mutual Life Insurance Co, Yasuda Mutual Life Insurance Co and Chiyoda Mutual Life Insurance Co.
